---
title: "Does a protective skin microbiome save the population?"
subtitle: "Building biological realism one step at a time"
engine: julia
---

## The question and the method

Amphibians can be treated with skin bacteria that inhibit the chytrid fungi *Batrachochytrium
dendrobatidis* (Bd) and *B. salamandrivorans* (Bsal). Would that protect a population?

The answer a model gives depends on how much biology is in it. This vignette makes that
dependence visible. For each of three host–pathogen systems it:

1. starts from the **simplest model** of the host and the pathogen;
2. adds the **biology of the host and pathogen** one piece at a time, with no treatment;
3. adds the **biology of the treatment** one piece at a time;
4. after every step, records the same two outcomes: the population **without treatment**, and
   the population under one fixed **reference treatment**;
5. ends with **chance**: the last model of each part is run again with whole animals and
   random events, many times over.

Every step keeps everything before it and changes one thing. Most steps add a piece of
biology; a few replace a placeholder with a more realistic version of the same piece (blocking
infection with the effect seen in trials, a fixed "treated" state with bacteria that decline).
The equations at the start of each part list the settings every step uses.
The final sections measure how much each addition moved the answer, and check with a factorial
design whether the effect of one piece of realism depends on the others. A
[second vignette](../02_nested_model/02_nested_model.md) repeats the exercise in a single
nested model, where every combination of pieces can be compared like for like.

| Part | System | Simplest model |
|---|---|---|
| A | Bsal in fire salamanders | susceptible and infectious adults |
| B | Bd in common toads | Mitchell et al. (2008) pond model |
| C | Bd in frogs | Briggs et al. (2010) load model |

::: {.callout-important}
The published models (Schmidt et al. 2017, Mitchell et al. 2008, Briggs et al. 2010) are
reproduced from their papers. Everything added to them is new work in this package and **is
not a published result**. Values taken from experiments are read from the package's parameter
compendium and are named where they are used. All other added values (efficacy, coverage,
spread, exposure windows, clearance) are illustrative: they show what the model does, not what
a real treatment would achieve.
:::

```{julia}
using Chytridiomycosis, Plots, Printf
using Distributions: LogNormal, quantile
using Random: Xoshiro, shuffle
default(linewidth = 2, size = (720, 380), legendfontsize = 8, guidefontsize = 9,
    titlefontsize = 10, left_margin = 4Plots.mm, bottom_margin = 4Plots.mm)

include("../diagram.jl")
T(; kw...) = MicrobiomeTreatment(; kw...)

# One row per step, filled in as we go. `untreated` and `treated` are the two outcomes;
# NaN where one does not apply.
ladder = NamedTuple[]
function step!(system, phase, added, untreated, treated, note)
    n = count(r -> r.system == system, ladder)
    push!(ladder, (; system, n, phase, added, untreated, treated, note))
    return (step = n, untreated = round(untreated, digits = 3), treated = round(treated, digits = 3))
end

function ladder_plot(system, xlabel)
    rows = filter(r -> r.system == system, ladder)
    k = length(rows)
    labels = ["$(r.n). $(r.added)" for r in rows]
    z(x) = isnan(x) ? 0.0 : x
    bar((1:k) .- 0.2, [z(r.untreated) for r in rows]; orientation = :h, bar_width = 0.38,
        label = "no treatment", color = :gray70, yticks = (1:k, labels), yflip = true, xlabel,
        xlims = (0, 1.05), xticks = 0:0.25:1, size = (840, 80 + 36k), left_margin = 6Plots.mm,
        legend = :outertop, legend_column = 2)
    bar!((1:k) .+ 0.2, [z(r.treated) for r in rows]; orientation = :h, bar_width = 0.38,
        label = "with treatment", color = :steelblue)
end
```

## Part A. Bsal in fire salamanders

The outcome in Part A is the **mean number of adults over the ten years after Bsal arrives,
as a fraction of carrying capacity**. The reference treatment is: every adult treated once,
on the day Bsal arrives, with bacteria that block 99% of infections for life.

### Host and pathogen

#### Step 0. Susceptible and infectious adults

The simplest model: an adult is susceptible or infectious, infection passes by contact, and
infectious animals die of the disease. This is the model of Schmidt et al. (2017) with its
latent period made negligibly short.

```{julia}
p = SchmidtParameters(:schmidt2017)
p_si = Chytridiomycosis.with(p; e = 5000.0)          # latent period under two hours
block = T(efficacy = 0.99)

sli(q, tr; kw...) = solve(ProbioticSLIProblem(q, tr; kw...))
u0, t0 = sli(p_si, T()), sli(p_si, block; coverage = 1.0)
@printf("R0 = %.1f\n", basic_reproduction_number(p_si))
step!("Bsal", "host", "susceptible and infectious adults", u0.mean_hosts, t0.mean_hosts,
    "collapse; treated adults live but are not replaced")
```

#### Step 1. A latent period

Infected animals are not infectious at once (Schmidt et al. 2017, as published).

```{julia}
u1, t1 = sli(p, T()), sli(p, block; coverage = 1.0)
@printf("R0 = %.1f\n", basic_reproduction_number(p))
step!("Bsal", "host", "+ latent period (Schmidt 2017)", u1.mean_hosts, t1.mean_hosts,
    "almost no change: a one-day delay against a one-week illness")
```

```{julia}
plot(u1.t, u1.hosts ./ p.K; label = "no treatment", xlabel = "years since Bsal arrived",
    ylabel = "adults (fraction of K)")
plot!(t1.t, t1.hosts ./ p.K; label = "all adults treated once")
plot!(t1.t, t1.treated ./ p.K; label = "of which still treated", linestyle = :dash)
```

Treated adults survive, but the population still declines: recruits are born untreated and
Bsal is still circulating.

#### Step 2. A larval stage

Salamanders have aquatic larvae. Here they are added as a stage that Bsal does not infect.

```{julia}
clean_larvae = BsalLarvalStage(carry_over = 0.0)
lar(st, tr; kw...) = solve(ProbioticLarvalProblem(p, st, tr; kw...))
u2, t2 = lar(clean_larvae, T()), lar(clean_larvae, block; coverage = 1.0)
step!("Bsal", "host", "+ larval stage, not infected", u2.mean_adults, t2.mean_adults,
    "untreated population no longer vanishes: larvae are a refuge")
```

```{julia}
plot(u1.t, max.(u1.hosts ./ p.K, 1e-12); yscale = :log10, label = "adults only (step 1)",
    xlabel = "years since Bsal arrived", ylabel = "adults (fraction of K), no treatment",
    legend = :bottomright)
plot!(u2.t, u2.adults ./ p.K; label = "with a larval stage (step 2)")
```

Larvae already in the water metamorphose after the adult epidemic has burnt out. The
near-extinction in the adults-only model was partly a result of having no other stage.

#### Step 3. Larvae can be infected

Fire salamander larvae can be infected experimentally without showing disease, and half
carried the infection through metamorphosis (Wang et al. 2021; the count is read from the
compendium). The transmission rate from adults to larvae is illustrative.

```{julia}
stage = BsalLarvalStage(:wang2021; adult_to_larva = 5.2)
@printf("carry-over through metamorphosis: %.1f; R0 = %.1f\n", stage.carry_over,
    basic_reproduction_number(p, stage))
u3, t3 = lar(stage, T()), lar(stage, block; coverage = 1.0)
step!("Bsal", "host", "+ larvae infected, carry-over 0.5", u3.mean_adults, t3.mean_adults,
    "small change at this carry-over")
```

This is the host model used for the rest of Part A.

#### The host model in equations

Densities are adult females and larvae per hectare; time is in years. Steps 0 and 1 use
`ProbioticSLIProblem`, which has adults only. Step 1 is the model of Schmidt et al. (2017):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dS}{dt} &= b S - (d + \gamma N) S - \beta S I \\
\frac{dL}{dt} &= \beta S I - (d + e + \gamma N) L \\
\frac{dI}{dt} &= e L - (d + d_I + \gamma N) I
\end{aligned}
$$

with $N = S + L + I$ and $\gamma = (b - d)/K$, so that without Bsal $S$ settles at $K$. Only
susceptible adults breed. Bsal enters as $I = 0.01$ per hectare (one per square kilometre) at $t = 0$.

- **Step 0** is the same system with $e = 5000$ per year, so that $L$ empties within hours and
  the model is in effect $S \to I$. The printed $R_0 = \beta e K / ((b + e)(b + d_I))$, which
  tends to $\beta K / (b + d_I)$ as $e$ grows.
- **Step 1** sets $e$ to its published value: a latent period of about one day.

Steps 2 and 3 use `ProbioticLarvalProblem`, which adds uninfected and infected larvae,
$W_S$ and $W_I$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dW_S}{dt} &= b' S - (m + \mu_W) W_S - \beta_{WA} I W_S \\
\frac{dW_I}{dt} &= \beta_{WA} I W_S - (m + \mu_W) W_I \\
\frac{dS}{dt} &= m W_S + (1 - c)\, m W_I - (d + \gamma N) S - \beta S I \\
\frac{dL}{dt} &= c\, m W_I + \beta S I - (d + e + \gamma N) L \\
\frac{dI}{dt} &= e L - (d + d_I + \gamma N) I
\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2** replaces the recruitment term $b S$ in $dS/dt$ with births into the larval
  stage, $b' S$ with $b' = b (m + \mu_W)/m$. Larvae leave by metamorphosis at rate $m$ or die
  at rate $\mu_W$. The choice of $b'$ keeps the Bsal-free state of step 1 ($S = K$, plus
  $W_S = bK/m$ larvae). Here $\beta_{WA} = 0$ and $c = 0$, so $W_I$ stays at zero.
- **Step 3** adds infection of larvae by infectious adults ($\beta_{WA} I W_S$) and carry-over:
  an infected larva becomes a latent adult with probability $c$, and a susceptible adult
  otherwise. Infected larvae do not die of Bsal and, in Part A, infect no one. (The code also
  has larva-to-larva and larva-to-adult transmission, `larva_to_larva` and `larva_to_adult`;
  both are zero throughout Part A.) The printed $R_0$ is the largest eigenvalue of the
  next-generation matrix for $(W_I, L, I)$ at the Bsal-free state.

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The host model after step 3. Solid arrows are flows, labelled with the per-capita rate; dashed arrows show who breeds and who infects whom. Not drawn: every adult class also dies at rate d + γN and every larval class at the larval death rate."
diagram("""
digraph {
  birth [label = "", shape = point, width = 0.06];
  subgraph cluster_larvae {
    label = "larvae"; style = "rounded"; color = "#999999";
    WS [label = <W<font point-size="8">S</font><br/>uninfected>];
    WI [label = <W<font point-size="8">I</font><br/>infected>, fillcolor = "#fde9c9"];
  }
  subgraph cluster_adults {
    label = "adults"; style = "rounded"; color = "#999999";
    S [label = "S\nsusceptible"];
    L [label = "L\nlatent", fillcolor = "#fde9c9"];
    I [label = "I\ninfectious", fillcolor = "#f4c7c3"];
  }
  dead [label = "", shape = point, width = 0.06];
  birth -> WS [label = "b′ S"];
  WS -> WI [label = <β<font point-size="7">WA</font> I>];
  WS -> S [label = "m"];
  WI -> S [label = "(1 − c) m"];
  WI -> L [label = "c m"];
  S -> L [label = "β I"];
  L -> I [label = "e"];
  I -> dead [label = <d<font point-size="7">I</font>>];
  S -> birth [style = dashed, color = "#888888", constraint = false, label = "breed"];

}
""")
```

| Symbol | Meaning | Value or source |
|---|---|---|
| $S, L, I$ | susceptible, latent and infectious adults (per ha) | start at $S = K$ |
| $W_S, W_I$ | uninfected and infected larvae (per ha) | start at $W_S = bK/m$ |
| $b$ | recruitment rate | 0.39 per yr, compendium (schmidt2017) |
| $d$ | natural death rate | 0.125 per yr, compendium (schmidt2017) |
| $d_I$ | death rate from Bsal | 52 per yr, compendium (schmidt2017) |
| $e$ | latent to infectious | 364 per yr, compendium (schmidt2017); 5000 in step 0 |
| $\beta$ | transmission between adults | 52 ha per yr, compendium (schmidt2017) |
| $K$ | carrying capacity | 25 per ha, compendium (schmidt2017) |
| $\gamma$ | density dependence | $(b - d)/K$ |
| $m$ | metamorphosis rate, 1/larval period | 1/0.33 per yr, illustrative |
| $\mu_W$ | larval death rate | 1 per yr, illustrative |
| $b'$ | larvae born per susceptible adult | $b (m + \mu_W)/m$ |
| $\beta_{WA}$ | transmission from adults to larvae | 0 in step 2; 5.2 ha per yr in step 3, illustrative |
| $c$ | carry-over through metamorphosis | 0 in step 2; 0.5 in step 3, compendium (wang2021: 5 of 10 larvae) |

The outcome is the mean of $(S + L + I)/K$ over the ten years after Bsal arrives.

### Treatment

The reference treatment of step 3 is now made more realistic. Each step states what changed.

#### The treatment in equations

Every class is split into untreated ($U$) and treated ($T$). With all treatment terms
present, the model of `ProbioticLarvalProblem` is, for adults,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dS_U}{dt} &= m\,[W_{SU} + (1 - r) W_{ST}] + (1 - c)\, m\,[W_{IU} + (1 - r) W_{IT}] \\
&\quad - (d + \gamma N) S_U - \lambda_A S_U + \omega S_T - a_A S_U \\
\frac{dS_T}{dt} &= r\, m W_{ST} + (1 - c)\, r\, m W_{IT} - (d + \gamma N) S_T - (1 - \varepsilon) \lambda_A S_T - \omega S_T + a_A S_U \\
\frac{dL_U}{dt} &= c\, m\,[W_{IU} + (1 - r) W_{IT}] + \lambda_A S_U - (d + e + \gamma N) L_U + \omega L_T - a_A L_U \\
\frac{dL_T}{dt} &= c\, r\, m W_{IT} + (1 - \varepsilon) \lambda_A S_T - (d + e + \gamma N) L_T - \omega L_T + a_A L_U \\
\frac{dI_U}{dt} &= e L_U - (d + d_I + \gamma N) I_U + \omega I_T - a_A I_U \\
\frac{dI_T}{dt} &= e L_T - (d + (1 - \tau) d_I + \gamma N) I_T - \omega I_T + a_A I_U
\end{aligned}
$$

and for larvae

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dW_{SU}}{dt} &= b'\,[S_U + S_T + \tau (L_T + I_T)] - (m + \mu_W) W_{SU} - \lambda_W W_{SU} + \omega W_{ST} - a_W W_{SU} \\
\frac{dW_{ST}}{dt} &= -(m + \mu_W) W_{ST} - (1 - \varepsilon) \lambda_W W_{ST} - \omega W_{ST} + a_W W_{SU} \\
\frac{dW_{IU}}{dt} &= \lambda_W W_{SU} - (m + \mu_W) W_{IU} + \omega W_{IT} - a_W W_{IU} \\
\frac{dW_{IT}}{dt} &= (1 - \varepsilon) \lambda_W W_{ST} - (m + \mu_W) W_{IT} - \omega W_{IT} + a_W W_{IU}
\end{aligned}
$$

with $N$ all adults and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda_A &= \beta\,[I_U + (1 - \sigma) I_T], \qquad \lambda_W = \beta_{WA}\,[I_U + (1 - \sigma) I_T], \\
a_A &= \eta\, \frac{S_T + L_T + I_T}{N}, \qquad a_W = \eta\, \frac{W_{ST} + W_{IT}}{W_{SU} + W_{ST} + W_{IU} + W_{IT}}, \\
\omega &= \frac{\ln 2}{h}, \qquad (\varepsilon, \tau, \sigma) = g(t - t_k)\,(\varepsilon_0, \tau_0, \sigma_0), \qquad g(a) = \frac{1 + 1/F}{1 + 2^{a/h_B}/F}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Treatment itself is a pulse. At each treatment time $t_k$, a fraction $\phi$ (`coverage`) of
every untreated class of the treated stage moves to the matching treated class, and the clock
of $g$ restarts ($t_k$ is the most recent application). Bsal arrives just after any treatment
at the same time. Recruits are born untreated. In steps 0 and 1 (`ProbioticSLIProblem`, no
larvae) the adult equations are the same without the metamorphosis terms, and recruits
$b\,[S_U + S_T + \tau (L_T + I_T)]$ enter $S_U$ directly. Treated, infected adults breed in
proportion to $\tau$: this is an assumption of the code, and with $\tau = 0$ it is Schmidt's
rule. (The code also has an environmental route of spread, `environmental`, and inheritance
from treated mothers, `maternal`; both are zero throughout Part A and are left out above.)

What each step switches on:

- **Steps 0–3, reference treatment**: `efficacy = 0.99`, adults treated once at $t = 0$ with
  $\phi = 1$. So $\varepsilon_0 = 0.99$ and $\omega = \eta = \tau_0 = \sigma_0 = 0$, $g = 1$:
  treated adults are infected at 1% of the untreated rate, for life.
- **Step 4**, `half_life = 1.0`: $\omega = \ln 2$ per year; treated animals revert to
  untreated.
- **Step 5**, `direct = 50.0`: $\eta = 50$ per year. An untreated animal acquires the bacteria
  in proportion to the treated fraction of its own stage. The vignette prints the microbiome's
  reproduction number $R_m = \eta/(\omega + b)$, with adult turnover $b$, and the long-run
  coverage $1 - 1/R_m$. Larvae are never treated in this step, so recruits acquire the bacteria
  only from adults.
- **Step 6**, `tolerance = 0.9` and no `efficacy`: $\varepsilon_0 = 0$, $\tau_0 = 0.9$. A treated,
  infected adult dies of Bsal at $(1 - \tau) d_I$, stays infectious, and breeds at $\tau$. The
  printed reproduction number, with all adults treated, is
  $R_0\,[1 - \phi + \phi M]$ with
  $M = (1 - \varepsilon)(1 - \sigma)(b + d_I)/(b + (1 - \tau) d_I)$. This uses the adults-only
  model and ignores gain or loss of the bacteria during an infection.
- **Step 7**, `load_reducing_treatment` with reduction in load $\rho$ and `death_exponent` $k$: $\sigma_0 = \rho$ and
  $\tau_0 = 1 - (1 - \rho)^k$, with $\varepsilon_0 = 0$. The run uses $\rho = 0.99$, $k = 1$,
  so $\sigma_0 = \tau_0 = 0.99$; loss and spread as in step 5.
- **Step 8**: the treatment of step 7, with `treat = :larvae` or `:both`, which applies the
  pulse to $W_{SU} \to W_{ST}$ and $W_{IU} \to W_{IT}$ as well, every quarter; `retention` is
  $r$. Treated larvae shed less, through $\sigma$ in $\lambda_A$ and $\lambda_W$; larvae do not
  die of Bsal, so tolerance does nothing for them.
- **Step 9**, `abundance_half_life = 5/365`, `protective_fold = 100`, on top of step 8: $g$ is
  no longer 1. It multiplies $\varepsilon_0$, $\tau_0$ and $\sigma_0$ (here $\tau_0$ and
  $\sigma_0$), falls to one half about $\log_2 F$ abundance half-lives after each application,
  and is reset to 1 by the next. All treated animals share one clock. The loss of step 4
  ($\omega$) and the spread of step 5 ($\eta$) stay.

| Symbol | Meaning | Value or source |
|---|---|---|
| $U, T$ | untreated, treated | |
| $\varepsilon_0$ | `efficacy`: reduction in the infection rate | 0.99 in steps 0–5; 0 from step 6; illustrative |
| $\tau_0$ | `tolerance`: reduction in death from Bsal | 0.9 in step 6; 0.99 from step 7; illustrative |
| $\sigma_0$ | `shedding_reduction`: reduction in shedding | 0.99 from step 7; illustrative |
| $h$, $\omega$ | `half_life` of treatment and loss rate $\ln 2 / h$ | $h$ = 1 yr from step 4, before that none ($\omega = 0$); illustrative |
| $\eta$ | `direct`: spread of the bacteria | 50 per yr from step 5, before that 0; illustrative |
| $\phi$ | `coverage` at each treatment | 1 |
| $t_k$ | `treat_times` | 0 in steps 0–7; every quarter from 0 to 9.75 yr in steps 8–9 (monthly in one run) |
| $r$ | `retention` at metamorphosis | 0 or 1 in step 8, 1 in step 9; illustrative, not measured |
| $h_B$ | `abundance_half_life` of the applied bacteria | 5 days in step 9, from this project's fits to Knapp et al. (2022) and Madison et al. (2025) |
| $F$ | `protective_fold` | 100 in step 9 (10 and 1000 in the plot); illustrative, not measured |
| $g$ | `protection`: share of the full effect left after time $a$ | 1 except in step 9 |

#### Step 4. Protection is lost

A treated animal reverts to untreated, with a half-life of one year.

```{julia}
a = lar(stage, T(efficacy = 0.99, half_life = 1.0); coverage = 1.0)
step!("Bsal", "treatment", "+ protection lost, half-life 1 year", u3.mean_adults, a.mean_adults,
    "collapse only delayed")
```

#### Step 5. The bacteria spread between animals

Treated animals pass the bacteria to others, so protection can reach the recruits.

```{julia}
spread = T(efficacy = 0.99, half_life = 1.0, direct = 50.0)
@printf("microbiome reproduction number %.0f, long-run coverage %.2f\n",
    microbiome_reproduction_number(spread; turnover = p.b), equilibrium_coverage(spread; turnover = p.b))
a = lar(stage, spread; coverage = 1.0)
step!("Bsal", "treatment", "+ bacteria spread between animals", u3.mean_adults, a.mean_adults,
    "full protection: the microbiome maintains itself")
```

A model stopped here says: **a self-spreading, strongly protective microbiome works, and
nothing else does.**

#### Step 6. What trials show: survival, not fewer infections

In challenge trials, treated animals were infected as often as untreated ones, but fewer
died. The compendium holds the counts from one trial in *Rana muscosa* (Harris et al. 2009):

```{julia}
h = parameter_set(:harris2009ismej)
mortality_reduction(h.deaths_treated, h.n_treated, h.deaths_control, h.n_control; rng = Xoshiro(1))
```

So the mechanism is changed: treatment reduces disease-induced death (`tolerance`) and does
not block infection. A treated, infected animal stays infectious. Loss and spread are as in
step 5.

```{julia}
tolerant = T(tolerance = 0.9, half_life = 1.0, direct = 50.0)
@printf("Bsal reproduction number if everyone is treated: %.0f (untreated %.0f)\n",
    effective_reproduction_number(p, tolerant, 1.0), basic_reproduction_number(p))
a = lar(stage, tolerant; coverage = 1.0)
step!("Bsal", "treatment", "mechanism as in trials: survive, still infected", u3.mean_adults,
    a.mean_adults, "fails; survivors shed for longer, so transmission rises")
```

#### Step 7. Lower load: less death and less shedding

Bacteria that suppress the fungus should lower the load on the animal, and so reduce shedding
as well as death. Both now follow from one reduction in load: shedding in proportion to load,
death in proportion to load raised to a power `k`.

```{julia}
reductions = [0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999]
ks = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0]
R = [effective_reproduction_number(p, load_reducing_treatment(ρ; death_exponent = k), 1.0)
     for ρ in reductions, k in ks]
plot(string.(reductions), R; yscale = :log10, marker = :circle, xlabel = "reduction in load",
    ylabel = "Bsal reproduction number, all treated",
    label = permutedims(["k = $k" for k in ks]), legend = :topright)
hline!([1.0]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "threshold")
```

With death proportional to load (`k = 1`) the two effects nearly cancel: the animal sheds less
but for longer.

```{julia}
a = lar(stage, load_reducing_treatment(0.99; half_life = 1.0, direct = 50.0); coverage = 1.0)
step!("Bsal", "treatment", "+ lower load (99%): also less shedding", u3.mean_adults, a.mean_adults,
    "partial; survivors remain infected")
```

#### Step 8. Treat larvae as well

With larvae in the host model they can be treated too. Whether a treated larva keeps the
bacteria through metamorphosis (`retention`) has not been measured. The treatment is that of
step 7: it lowers the load, is lost with a half-life of a year, and spreads.

```{julia}
quarterly = 0:0.25:9.75
step7 = load_reducing_treatment(0.99; half_life = 1.0, direct = 50.0)
options = [("adults, once", (;)),
    ("larvae, quarterly; lost at metamorphosis", (treat = :larvae, treat_times = quarterly)),
    ("larvae, quarterly; kept", (treat = :larvae, treat_times = quarterly, retention = 1.0)),
    ("both stages, quarterly; kept", (treat = :both, treat_times = quarterly, retention = 1.0))]
vals = [lar(stage, step7; coverage = 1.0, kw...).mean_adults for (_, kw) in options]
bar(vals; orientation = :h, yticks = (1:4, first.(options)), yflip = true, legend = false,
    xlabel = "mean adults (fraction of K)", xlims = (0, 1.05), xticks = 0:0.25:1,
    left_margin = 6Plots.mm, size = (820, 230), color = :steelblue)
```

```{julia}
both_block = lar(stage, block; coverage = 1.0, treat = :both, treat_times = quarterly, retention = 1.0)
@printf("the same schedule with bacteria that block infection and last: %.2f\n", both_block.mean_adults)
step!("Bsal", "treatment", "+ treat both stages, kept through metamorphosis", u3.mean_adults, vals[4],
    "little gain: treated animals still carry and pass on Bsal")
```

Treating larvae as well barely helps, because with this mechanism a treated animal is still
infected and still transmits. The same schedule with bacteria that block infection and last
would protect the population fully with no spread at all (printed above). Whether treating
larvae is worth doing depends on what the bacteria do, a dependence the factorial below
measures.

#### Step 9. How long the bacteria really last

Two open datasets (a field trial in *Rana sierrae*, Knapp et al. 2022, and a laboratory trial
in *Xenopus laevis*, Madison et al. 2025) give the abundance of applied bacteria over time.
Fitting an exponential decline gives half-lives of 3 to 14 days, and 4 to 5 days in the field.
(The fits are this project's own.) Protection now wanes with abundance. `protective_fold` is
how far abundance can fall before half the effect is lost; it has not been measured.

```{julia}
days = 0:1:150
plot(xlabel = "days since application", ylabel = "fraction of full protection", legend = :topright)
for F in (10.0, 100.0, 1000.0)
    w = T(efficacy = 0.99, abundance_half_life = 5 / 365, protective_fold = F)
    plot!(days, [protection(w, d / 365) for d in days];
        label = @sprintf("fold %g: half gone after %.0f days", F, 365 * protection_duration(w)))
end
current()
```

```{julia}
waning = load_reducing_treatment(0.99; half_life = 1.0, direct = 50.0,
    abundance_half_life = 5 / 365, protective_fold = 100.0)
a = lar(stage, waning; coverage = 1.0, treat = :both, treat_times = quarterly, retention = 1.0)
monthly = lar(stage, waning; coverage = 1.0, treat = :both, treat_times = 0:(1 / 12):9.95, retention = 1.0)
@printf("dosed monthly instead of quarterly: %.2f\n", monthly.mean_adults)
step!("Bsal", "treatment", "+ fitted decay (half-life 5 days)", u3.mean_adults, a.mean_adults,
    "fails: protection lasts about a month")
```

#### Step 10. Chance

Every model so far treats animals as continuous densities, so a population, or Bsal, can be
reduced to a fraction of an animal and grow back. The last step runs the same model with
whole animals and random events (`StochasticNestedProblem`, which reproduces the equations
when the population is large). Bsal arrives as one infected adult in 20 hectares, 500 adults,
and each case is run 100 times.

In the stochastic version each class holds a whole number of animals in an area of 20 ha:
500 adults ($K \times 20$) and 64 larvae ($bK/m \times 20$) at the start. Every term of the
equations above becomes a per-animal rate, evaluated at densities (count divided by area).
In each step of six hours ($\Delta t = 1/1460$ yr) an animal leaves its class with
probability $1 - e^{-R \Delta t}$, where $R$ is the sum of its rates out, and goes to each
destination with probability in proportion to that rate. Births are Poisson, with mean the
birth term of the equations times the area times $\Delta t$. A treatment treats each
untreated animal with probability $\phi$. The transitions come from the package's nested
model (`NestedChytridProblem`); with the latent class, larvae and larval infection switched
on, as here, they are the equations above, so the two versions agree when the area is large.
One difference from the equations: one infected adult in 20 ha is 0.05 per ha, against 0.01
per ha in steps 0–9.

```{julia}
using Random: Xoshiro
host_a = ChytridBiology(:wang2021; latent = true, larvae = true, larval_infection = true)
chanceA(tr; kw...) = [solve(StochasticNestedProblem(p, host_a, tr; area = 20.0, kw...); rng = Xoshiro(s))
    for s in 1:100]
meanA(rs) = sum(r.mean_adults for r in rs) / length(rs)
cu = chanceA(T())
ct = chanceA(waning; coverage = 1.0, treat = :both, treat_times = quarterly, retention = 1.0)
cb = chanceA(block; coverage = 1.0)
@printf("Bsal lost within 10 years, untreated: %d of 100 runs\n", count(r -> !isnan(r.pathogen_extinction), cu))
@printf("reference treatment of step 3 (block 99%%, adults once): %.2f with chance, %.2f in the equations\n",
    meanA(cb), t3.mean_adults)
step!("Bsal", "chance", "+ chance: whole animals, 20 ha", meanA(cu), meanA(ct),
    "still fails: treated animals are infected and pass Bsal on")
```

For the final treatment chance changes little. Treated animals are infected as readily as
untreated ones, so Bsal establishes and the population collapses before Bsal is lost. Chance
matters a great deal for the step-3 reference treatment, which blocks infection: with whole
animals, Bsal arriving in a population that has just been treated usually fails to establish
and is lost, and does not come back, so that treatment keeps nearly the whole population
instead of a third. The [second vignette](../02_nested_model/02_nested_model.md) explores this
in detail.

### Part A summary

```{julia}
ladder_plot("Bsal", "mean adults over 10 years, fraction of K")
```

## Part B. Bd in common toads

The outcome in Part B is the **number of adults in years 25 to 35 after Bd arrives, as a
fraction of the number without Bd**. The reference treatment is: 80% of tadpoles treated at
hatching every year with bacteria that block 90% of infections for the season. The parameter
set is the one behind Figure 2d of Mitchell et al. (2008).

### Host and pathogen

#### Step 0. The pond model

Mitchell's model is the simplest available for this system, though it is not as simple as
step 0 of Part A: tadpoles are infected by zoospores in the pond, infected tadpoles are
removed at metamorphosis, and juveniles and adults are never infected.

The equations below are the host model as it stands after step 3. Time $t$ is in years and
$T$ is the time of year. Between the yearly events,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dP_X}{dt} &= -(\mu_P + \nu Z)\,P_X \\
\frac{dP_Y}{dt} &= \nu Z\,P_X - (\mu_P + \alpha_P)\,P_Y \\
\frac{dM}{dt} &= -(\mu_J + \varepsilon)\,M \\
\frac{dA_X}{dt} &= \varepsilon M \left(1 - \frac{A_X + A_Y}{K}\right) - \mu_A A_X
  - \chi(t)\,\nu_A Z A_X + \sigma_A A_Y \\
\frac{dA_Y}{dt} &= \chi(t)\,\nu_A Z A_X - (\mu_A + \alpha_A + \sigma_A)\,A_Y \\
\frac{dZ}{dt} &= \rho P_Y + \chi(t)\,\rho_A A_Y + \gamma Z e^{-\varphi Z} - \mu_Z Z
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\chi(t) = 1$ while adults are at the pond ($t_1 \le T < t_1 + d_A/365$) and 0 otherwise.
Three events happen each year:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T = t_1 &: \quad P_X \leftarrow P_X + \iota\psi\,(A_X + A_Y) \\
T = t_2 &: \quad J_0 = P_X\,(1 - q + q\,s_J) + P_Y\,s_J, \qquad
  q = 1 - e^{-\nu Z d_J / 365}, \qquad P_X,\ P_Y \leftarrow 0 \\
\omega \text{ after } t_2 &: \quad M \leftarrow M + J_0\,e^{-\mu_J \omega}
\end{aligned}
$$

At breeding, tadpoles are born to every adult. At metamorphosis the tadpoles leave the pond as
a juvenile cohort $J_0$; $Z$ in $q$ is its value at that moment. A cohort only dies (at rate $\mu_J$) until it is $\omega$ old, and then
joins the pool $M$ of juveniles that can mature into adults. $M$ is Mitchell's
$\int_\omega^\infty J\,da$: following each cohort in closed form solves the paper's
age-structured juvenile equation exactly.

| Step | What it adds | Terms |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Mitchell et al. (2008), equations (2.1) to (2.5) | $s_J = 0$, $d_J = 0$, no $A_Y$ ($\chi = 0$) |
| 1 | infected metamorphs can survive | $s_J > 0$ |
| 2 | metamorphs are exposed as they leave | $d_J > 0$, so $q > 0$ |
| 3 | adults are infected at the pond, shed there and clear the infection | $A_Y$, $\chi(t)$, $\nu_A$, $\rho_A$, $\sigma_A$ |

With steps 1 to 3 switched off, the equations are those of Mitchell et al. (2008), and the
package reproduces the outcomes of their Fig. 2b to 2d. Bd arrives as $Z_0$ zoospores at the
start of year 0, after 100 years without Bd. Following the paper, the toads are declared extinct
(every stage set to zero) below 50 adults, and Bd below 100 zoospores. The package tests the
toads at each yearly event, and Bd only at breeding, when there are no tadpoles. In step 3 Bd is
not removed at breeding while an infected adult is present.

| Symbol | Meaning | Value or source |
|---|---|---|
| $P_X$, $P_Y$ | uninfected and infected tadpoles | |
| $J_0$, $M$ | a juvenile cohort at metamorphosis; juveniles older than $\omega$ | |
| $A_X$, $A_Y$ | uninfected and infected adults | |
| $Z$ | free-living zoospores in the pond | |
| $t_1$, $t_2$ | day of breeding and of metamorphosis | days 60 and 155, compendium (mitchell2008) |
| $\omega$ | age at which juveniles can start to mature | 500 days, compendium (mitchell2008) |
| $\iota$, $\psi$ | mating couples per adult; eggs per couple | 0.14, 2000, compendium (mitchell2008) |
| $\varepsilon$ | maturation rate of juveniles older than $\omega$ | 0.16 per year, compendium (mitchell2008) |
| $\mu_P$, $\mu_J$, $\mu_A$ | natural death rates of tadpoles, juveniles, adults | 7.55, 0.73, 0.73 per year, compendium (mitchell2008) |
| $K$ | limit on the number of adults | 14,000, compendium (mitchell2008) |
| $\alpha_P$ | extra death rate of infected tadpoles | 1.62 per year, compendium (mitchell2008) |
| $\nu$ | infection rate per zoospore | $2.3 \times 10^{-8}$ per zoospore per year, compendium (mitchell2008, Fig. 2d) |
| $\rho$ | zoospores released per infected tadpole | $6 \times 10^{6}$ per tadpole per year, compendium (mitchell2008, Fig. 2d) |
| $\mu_Z$ | zoospore death rate | 13 per year, compendium (mitchell2008) |
| $\gamma$, $\varphi$ | saprobic growth of zoospores and its density dependence | 0 (so the term is off), $10^{-6}$, compendium (mitchell2008) |
| $Z_0$ | zoospores introduced | $10^4$, package default |
| $s_J$ | chance that an infected metamorph survives and clears Bd | 0 (step 0); $1 - 72/101 = 0.29$ from step 1, compendium (smith2022) |
| $d_J$ | days metamorphs are exposed as they leave | 0 (steps 0, 1); 7 from step 2, illustrative |
| $d_A$ | days adults spend at the pond from $t_1$ | 30 in step 3, illustrative |
| $\nu_A$, $\rho_A$ | adult infection rate and shedding while at the pond | equal to $\nu$ and $\rho$ in step 3, illustrative |
| $\sigma_A$ | adult clearance rate | 1 per year in step 3, illustrative |
| $\alpha_A$ | extra death rate of infected adults | 0, illustrative |

```{julia}

Breeding (day 60), metamorphosis (day 155) and maturation at age ω are yearly pulses; dashed arrows are shedding into and infection from the zoospore pool. $A = A_X + A_Y$."

```{julia}
m = MitchellParameters(:mitchell2008; set = "fig2d")
none = PostMetamorphicInfection()
pond(tr; stages = none, kw...) = solve(ProbioticPondProblem(m, tr; stages, kw...))
rel(r) = r.A_mean / r.A_disease_free
ref = T(efficacy = 0.9)

u, t = pond(T()), pond(ref; coverage = 0.8)
@printf("Bd persists: untreated %s, treated %s\n", u.bd_persist, t.bd_persist)
step!("Bd toad", "host", "Mitchell 2008 pond model", rel(u), rel(t),
    "untreated: toads and Bd both die out; treated: toads saved, Bd gone")
```

```{julia}
series(r) = (r.t[r.t .>= -2], r.A[r.t .>= -2] ./ r.A_disease_free)
plot(series(u)...; label = "no treatment", xlabel = "years since Bd arrived",
    ylabel = "adults (fraction of disease-free)", legend = :right)
plot!(series(t)...; label = "tadpoles treated every year")
```

Unlike Bsal, the simplest treatment works here: the infected stage is short and a new cohort
can be treated each year. It does not prevent the initial crash.

#### Step 1. Infected metamorphs can survive

Experiments show that toadlets exposed to Bd are infected, that most die, and that some
survive (Smith et al. 2022; counts from the compendium).

```{julia}
s = parameter_set(:smith2022)
survival = 1 - s.deaths_exposed / s.n_exposed
@printf("toadlet survival after exposure: %.2f\n", survival)
st1 = PostMetamorphicInfection(metamorph_survival = survival)
u, t = pond(T(); stages = st1), pond(ref; coverage = 0.8, stages = st1)
@printf("Bd persists: untreated %s, treated %s\n", u.bd_persist, t.bd_persist)
step!("Bd toad", "host", "+ infected metamorphs can survive (0.29)", rel(u), rel(t),
    "toads no longer die out, so nor does Bd; treatment now protects poorly")
```

One added survival probability reverses both outcomes. The published "both die out" result
depended on every infected animal dying; once some survive, the host persists, Bd persists
with it, and blocking 90% of infections is no longer enough.

#### Step 2. Metamorphs are exposed as they leave the pond

```{julia}
st2 = PostMetamorphicInfection(metamorph_survival = survival, metamorph_exposure_days = 7.0)
u, t = pond(T(); stages = st2), pond(ref; coverage = 0.8, stages = st2)
step!("Bd toad", "host", "+ metamorphs exposed for a week on leaving", rel(u), rel(t),
    "little further change")
```

#### Step 3. Adults carry Bd between years

Breeding adults carry Bd at low prevalence in field surveys. Here adults are infected while
at the pond, shed there, and clear the infection over about a year. Adults are never treated
(metamorphs lose the bacteria), so the treated tadpoles of the reference treatment now share
the pond with infected adults.

```{julia}
st3 = PostMetamorphicInfection(metamorph_survival = survival, metamorph_exposure_days = 7.0,
    adult_exposure_days = 30.0, adult_relative_shedding = 1.0, adult_clearance = 1.0)
r = solve(ToadStageProblem(m, st3))
@printf("Bd persists: %s; adult prevalence after breeding: %.2f\n", r.bd_persist, r.adult_prevalence)
u, t = pond(T(); stages = st3), pond(ref; coverage = 0.8, stages = st3)
@printf("the pond model with treatment, untreated: %.3f (stage model %.3f)\n", rel(u),
    r.A_mean / r.A_disease_free)
step!("Bd toad", "host", "+ adults carry Bd between years", rel(u), rel(t),
    "little change in this parameter set")
```

The host model of step 3 is used for the rest of Part B. With no treatment, the pond model
with treated classes reproduces the stage model exactly (printed above).

Every "with treatment" outcome in Part B, including the reference treatment of steps 0 to 2,
comes from the model below. From step 3 it sits on the step-3 host, with adults infected at
the pond as above; adults are never treated. Tadpoles are split into untreated ($U$) and
treated ($T$), uninfected and infected:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dP_{XU}}{dt} &= -(\mu_P + \nu Z)\,P_{XU} + \lambda P_{XT} \\
\frac{dP_{XT}}{dt} &= -\big(\mu_P + (1 - g\eta)\,\nu Z + \lambda\big)\,P_{XT} \\
\frac{dP_{YU}}{dt} &= \nu Z\,P_{XU} - (\mu_P + \alpha_P)\,P_{YU} + \lambda P_{YT} \\
\frac{dP_{YT}}{dt} &= (1 - g\eta)\,\nu Z\,P_{XT} - \big(\mu_P + (1 - g\tau)\,\alpha_P + \lambda\big)\,P_{YT} \\
\frac{dZ}{dt} &= \rho\,\big(P_{YU} + (1 - g\kappa)\,P_{YT}\big) + \chi\rho_A A_Y + \gamma Z e^{-\varphi Z} - \mu_Z Z
\end{aligned}
$$

with $M$, $A_X$ and $A_Y$ as in step 3 ($\chi = 1$ while adults are at the pond, and 0
otherwise; $A_Y = 0$ before step 3). A treated tadpole is infected less often (efficacy $\eta$), dies of
infection less often (tolerance $\tau$) and sheds less (shedding reduction $\kappa$). It loses
the bacteria at rate $\lambda = \ln 2 / h$. All three effects are scaled by the protection left
since the last dose, $g = g(t - t_{\mathrm{dose}})$, where

$$
g(a) = \frac{1 + 1/F}{1 + 2^{a/h_B}/F}.
$$

$g = 1$ when the bacteria do not decline ($h_B = \infty$). Treatment enters through three
events in each year from the arrival of Bd:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T = t_1 &: \quad P_{XU} \leftarrow P_{XU} + \iota\psi (A_X + A_Y), \quad \text{then}\quad
  P_{XT} \leftarrow P_{XT} + c\,P_{XU},\ \ P_{XU} \leftarrow (1 - c)\,P_{XU},\ \ t_{\mathrm{dose}} \leftarrow t \\
T = t_1 + d_k/365 &: \quad P_{iT} \leftarrow P_{iT} + c\,P_{iU},\ \ P_{iU} \leftarrow (1 - c)\,P_{iU}
  \ \ (i = X, Y),\ \ t_{\mathrm{dose}} \leftarrow t \\
T = t_2 &: \quad J_0 = P_{XU}(1 - q_U + q_U s_U) + P_{XT}(1 - q_T + q_T s_T) + P_{YU} s_U + P_{YT} s_T
\end{aligned}
$$

with $q_U = 1 - e^{-\nu Z d_J/365}$, $q_T = 1 - e^{-(1 - g\eta)\nu Z d_J/365}$, $s_U = s_J$ and
$s_T = s_J + g\tau(1 - s_J)$. Tolerance therefore also raises the survival of infected
metamorphs. Metamorphs lose the bacteria, so every juvenile and adult is untreated. With one
dose at hatching and $h_B = 5$ days, $F = 100$, the protection left at metamorphosis 95 days
later is $g = 1.01/(1 + 2^{19}/100) \approx 0.0002$. Each
extra dose also treats a share $c$ of the tadpoles still untreated, so after the dose at
hatching and four more, all but $0.2^5$ (about 0.03%) of tadpoles have been treated.

Each step keeps the treatment of the one before and changes one thing:

| Step | Treatment in the "with treatment" outcome |
|---|---|
| 0 to 3 (reference) | $\eta = 0.9$, $c = 0.8$, no loss of protection |
| 4 | + loss: $h = 0.05$ years (18 days) |
| 5 | $\tau = 0.7$ in place of $\eta$ (the effect seen in trials); loss as in step 4 |
| 6 | + lower shedding: $\tau = \kappa = 0.7$ (`load_reducing_treatment(0.7)`) |
| 7 | + protection declines with $h_B = 5$ days and $F = 100$; one dose |
| 8 | + doses also on days $d_k$ = 20, 40, 60 and 80 |
| 9 | + chance |

| Symbol | Meaning | Value or source |
|---|---|---|
| $c$ | share of untreated tadpoles treated at each dose | 0.8, illustrative |
| $\eta$ | efficacy: reduction in the infection rate | 0.9 (reference, step 4); 0.5, 0.9, 0.99 compared in step 5; illustrative |
| $\tau$ | tolerance: reduction in the extra death rate of infected tadpoles | 0.7 (steps 5 to 9); 0.3, 0.7, 1.0 compared in step 5; illustrative |
| $\kappa$ | shedding reduction | 0.7 from step 6 (load 70% lower, death proportional to load), illustrative |
| $h$, $\lambda$ | half-life of the treated state; $\lambda = \ln 2/h$ | 18 days from step 4, before that $\infty$; illustrative |
| $\chi$, $\rho_A$ | adults at the pond; their shedding rate | as in step 3 |
| $h_B$ | half-life of the applied bacteria | 5 days, this project's fit to Knapp et al. (2022) and Madison et al. (2025) (Part A, step 9) |
| $F$ | starting abundance over the abundance giving half the effect | 100, illustrative |
| $d_k$ | days after hatching of extra doses | 20, 40, 60, 80 in step 8, illustrative |
| $g$ | share of the full effect left since the last dose | from $h_B$ and $F$ |

The package can also spread the bacteria between tadpoles, through a pond reservoir, or from
treated mothers, and can treat adults instead. All of these are off in Part B.

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Treated tadpoles (steps 4 to 9). Each dose moves a share c of untreated tadpoles to the treated classes (doses after hatching from step 8); λ is loss of the bacteria (from step 4); g is the protection left since the last dose (from step 7). Juveniles and adults are as in the step-3 diagram, and all are untreated."
diagram("""
digraph {
  compound = true; ranksep = 0.55; forcelabels = true;
  hatch [shape = plaintext, style = "", label = <hatchlings<br/>ιψA, day 60>];
  subgraph cluster_pond {

### Treatment

#### Step 4. Protection is lost

```{julia}
a = pond(T(efficacy = 0.9, half_life = 0.05); coverage = 0.8, stages = st3)
step!("Bd toad", "treatment", "+ protection lost, half-life 18 days", rel(u), rel(a),
    "most of the small benefit lost")
```

#### Step 5. Mechanism as in trials: survival, not fewer infections

Treated tadpoles are now infected as often as untreated ones but survive better. The loss of
step 4 stays, for both mechanisms in the comparison.

```{julia}
effs, tols = [0.5, 0.9, 0.99], [0.3, 0.7, 1.0]
blocking = [rel(pond(T(efficacy = e, half_life = 0.05); coverage = 0.8, stages = st3)) for e in effs]
tolerating = [rel(pond(T(tolerance = τ, half_life = 0.05); coverage = 0.8, stages = st3)) for τ in tols]
plot(["weak", "medium", "strong"], blocking; marker = :circle,
    label = "blocks infection (0.5, 0.9, 0.99)", xlabel = "strength of treatment",
    ylabel = "adults (fraction of disease-free)", ylims = (0, 0.2), legend = :topleft)
plot!(["weak", "medium", "strong"], tolerating; marker = :square,
    label = "survives infection (0.3, 0.7, 1.0)")
```

```{julia}
a = pond(T(tolerance = 0.7, half_life = 0.05); coverage = 0.8, stages = st3)
step!("Bd toad", "treatment", "mechanism as in trials: survive, still infected", rel(u), rel(a),
    "better than blocking at every strength; Bd persists")
```

For Bsal the observed mechanism made treatment fail. Here it makes treatment work better,
because Bd is going to persist anyway and what matters is how many infected animals live. With
protection lost after a few weeks, though, neither mechanism does much.

#### Step 6. Lower load

```{julia}
a = pond(load_reducing_treatment(0.7; half_life = 0.05); coverage = 0.8, stages = st3)
step!("Bd toad", "treatment", "+ lower load (70%): also less shedding", rel(u), rel(a),
    "little changed: untreated tadpoles, adults and the pond keep Bd going")
```

#### Step 7. How long the bacteria really last

With the fitted decay (half-life 5 days), the protection of one dose at hatching wanes during
the 95-day tadpole season, on top of the loss of step 4.

```{julia}
waning_t = load_reducing_treatment(0.7; half_life = 0.05, abundance_half_life = 5 / 365,
    protective_fold = 100.0)
schedules = [("at hatching only", Float64[]), ("+ day 45", [45.0]), ("+ days 30, 60", [30.0, 60.0]),
    ("+ days 20, 40, 60, 80", [20.0, 40.0, 60.0, 80.0])]
doses = [rel(pond(waning_t; coverage = 0.8, stages = st3, redose_days = d)) for (_, d) in schedules]
bar(doses; orientation = :h, yticks = (1:4, first.(schedules)), yflip = true, legend = false,
    xlabel = "adults (fraction of disease-free)", xlims = (0, 1.05), xticks = 0:0.25:1,
    left_margin = 6Plots.mm, size = (820, 230), color = :steelblue)
```

```{julia}
step!("Bd toad", "treatment", "+ fitted decay, one dose at hatching", rel(u), doses[1],
    "protection gone before the season ends")
```

#### Step 8. Several doses in a season

```{julia}
step!("Bd toad", "treatment", "+ five doses per season", rel(u), doses[4],
    "the largest gain in Part B: about half the disease-free population")
```

Each dose renews the protection of treated tadpoles and also treats 80% of those still
untreated, infected ones included, so after five doses almost every tadpole has been treated.
Part of the benefit comes from that higher coverage, not only from renewed protection.

#### Step 9. Chance

The same pond model with every tadpole, toad and zoospore a whole number, and every event
random (`solve(problem; rng)`); 50 runs of each case. Mitchell et al.'s rule that toads are
extinct below 50 adults, and Bd below 100 zoospores, is no longer needed: each goes extinct
when its numbers reach zero.

In terms of the equations, every flow above becomes a random event, drawn in steps of one day
(tau-leaping). In each step every animal or zoospore leaves its class with probability
$1 - e^{-Rh}$, where $R$ is the sum of its per-capita rates out of that class and $h$ is one
day, and goes to each destination in proportion to that rate. New zoospores are a Poisson draw
with mean $\big(\rho\,(P_{YU} + (1 - g\kappa)P_{YT}) + \chi\rho_A A_Y\big)\,h$. The yearly events become draws as well:
hatchlings are Poisson with mean $\iota\psi A_X$, each dose treats a binomial share $c$ of
untreated tadpoles, and an uninfected, untreated metamorph reaches age $\omega$ with
probability $(1 - q_U + q_U s_U)\,e^{-\mu_J\omega}$ (likewise for the other classes). The limits of 50 adults and 100 zoospores are
not applied.

```{julia}
chanceB(tr; stages = st3, kw...) = [solve(ProbioticPondProblem(m, tr; stages, kw...); rng = Xoshiro(s)) for s in 1:50]
meanB(rs) = sum(rel(r) for r in rs) / length(rs)
five = (coverage = 0.8, redose_days = [20.0, 40.0, 60.0, 80.0])
bu, bt = chanceB(T()), chanceB(waning_t; five...)
base = chanceB(T(); stages = none)
blk = chanceB(ref; coverage = 0.8)
@printf("Mitchell's model (step 0), untreated: toads persist in %d of 50 runs, adults %.2f (equations: extinct)\n",
    count(r -> r.toads_persist, base), meanB(base))
@printf("reference treatment (block 90%%) on the step-3 host: %.2f, Bd persists in %d of 50 (equations: %.2f)\n",
    meanB(blk), count(r -> r.bd_persist, blk), rel(pond(ref; coverage = 0.8, stages = st3)))
step!("Bd toad", "chance", "+ chance: whole animals", meanB(bu), meanB(bt),
    "little change for this model; large changes elsewhere (see text)")
```

For the final model chance changes little. Elsewhere on the ladder it changes a great deal:

- **Mitchell's published outcome does not survive it.** In the equations Bd drives the toads
  to extinction and then dies out itself. With whole animals the toads fall to a few dozen
  adults, too few tadpoles remain to carry Bd through the winter, Bd is lost, and the toads
  recover. The published result depends on declaring toads extinct below 50 adults.
- **Blocking infection does better.** On the step-3 host model, Bd is lost by chance in some
  runs, and treatment then protects the population fully.

### Part B summary

```{julia}
ladder_plot("Bd toad", "adults in years 25 to 35, fraction of disease-free")
```

## Part C. Bd in frogs

The outcome in Part C is the **fraction of 80 frogs sharing one pool that are alive after two
years**. Disease here depends on the fungal load on each frog. Treatment is introduced at
step 3.

### Host and pathogen

#### Step 0. Load on each frog

In the model of Briggs et al. (2010) each frog carries a load of sporangia. Sporangia release
zoospores into a shared pool, zoospores infect frogs, and a frog dies when its load reaches a
lethal level. Loads run away when there are enough frogs to keep the pool topped up.

The equations below are the model as it stands after step 2. Each live frog $i$ carries
$S_i$ sporangia, and the pool holds $Z$ zoospores:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dS_i}{dt} &= \frac{\nu\gamma}{V}\,Z + (\eta\nu f - \sigma)\,S_i - \frac{c_i\,S_i}{h + S_i}, \\
\frac{dZ}{dt} &= \varepsilon + \eta(1 - f)\sum_{j\ \mathrm{alive}} S_j - \mu Z - \frac{\gamma}{V}\,N_{\mathrm{alive}}\,Z.
\end{aligned}
$$

Zoospores meet each frog at rate $\gamma/V$, and a fraction $\nu$ of meetings start a
sporangium. Each sporangium releases $\eta$ zoospores a day: a fraction $f$ reinfect the same
frog and the rest go to the pool. A frog dies when $S_i$ reaches $S_{\max}$; from then on it
sheds nothing and takes up no zoospores. All frogs start with no sporangia, and the pool
starts at $\varepsilon/(\mu + \gamma N/V)$. On its own a frog's load would decline, because
$\eta\nu f$ (about 0.04 per day) is below $\sigma$; loads run away only when enough frogs feed
the pool.

What each step adds:

- **Step 0** is the model of Briggs et al. (2010) with no clearance ($c_i = 0$). The
  $S_i$ and $Z$ equations without $\varepsilon$ are those of the paper. The outside input
  $\varepsilon$ is the paper's external source of zoospores (its Fig. 3D), here as a
  constant rate.
- **Step 1** adds clearance by the frog, $c\,S_i/(h + S_i)$, the same for every frog
  ($c_i = c$). This term is new in this package.
- **Step 2** lets $c_i$ differ: the 80 values are evenly spaced quantiles of a lognormal
  distribution with median $c$.

| Symbol | Meaning | Value or source |
|---|---|---|
| $S_i$ | sporangia on frog $i$ | state (sporangia per frog) |
| $Z$ | zoospores in the pool | state (zoospores per pool) |
| $N_{\mathrm{alive}}$ | frogs alive | starts at $N = 80$ |
| $V$ | pool volume | 1 volume unit; compendium (briggs2010) |
| $\gamma$ | rate at which zoospores meet a frog | 0.01 volume units per day; compendium (briggs2010) |
| $\nu$ | fraction of meetings that start a sporangium | 0.05; compendium (briggs2010) |
| $f$ | fraction of released zoospores that reinfect the same frog | 0.05; compendium (briggs2010) |
| $\eta$ | zoospores released per sporangium | 17.5 per day; compendium (briggs2010) |
| $\sigma$ | loss of sporangia | 0.2 per day; compendium (briggs2010) |
| $\mu$ | death of zoospores in the pool | 1 per day; compendium (briggs2010) |
| $S_{\max}$ | lethal load | 10,000 sporangia; compendium (briggs2010) |
| $\varepsilon$ | zoospores entering from outside | 1,000 per day; set in this vignette (the value Briggs et al. used for an external source) |
| $c$ | maximum clearance (step 1) | 100 sporangia per day; illustrative |
| $h$ | load at which clearance is half its maximum (step 1) | 500 sporangia; illustrative |
| $c_i$ | clearance of frog $i$ (step 2) | lognormal, median $c$, log-scale sd 0.5; illustrative |

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The load model for one frog $i$ and the shared zoospore pool. Clearance ($c_i$) is added in steps 1 and 2."
diagram("""
digraph {
  outside [label = "outside", shape = plaintext, style = ""];
  Z [label = "zoospores Z\\n(shared pool)", shape = ellipse, fillcolor = "#e2efda"];
  Si [label = <sporangia S<SUB>i</SUB><BR/>on frog i>];
  Sj [label = <other frogs S<SUB>j</SUB>>];
  lostZ [label = "lost", shape = plaintext, style = ""];
  lostS [label = "lost", shape = plaintext, style = ""];
  dead [label = <frog dies<BR/>at S<SUB>i</SUB> = S<SUB>max</SUB>>, fillcolor = "#f4cccc"];
  outside -> Z [label = "ε"];
  Z -> Si [label = "(νγ/V) Z"];
  Z -> Sj [label = "(νγ/V) Z"];
  Si -> Z [label = <η(1−f) S<SUB>i</SUB>>];
  Sj -> Z [label = <η(1−f) S<SUB>j</SUB>>];
  Si -> Si [label = <ηνf S<SUB>i</SUB>>];
  Z -> lostZ [label = "μZ + (γ/V) N Z"];
  Si -> lostS [label = <σS<SUB>i</SUB> + c<SUB>i</SUB>S<SUB>i</SUB>/(h + S<SUB>i</SUB>)>];
  Si -> dead [style = dashed, color = "#888888"];
}
""")
```

```{julia}
pb = BriggsParameters(:briggs2010)
N, hsat = 80, 500.0
ε = parameter_set(:briggs2010; set = "fig3d").εZ    # zoospores from outside, per day
tipping(c; n = N) = solve(LoadTippingProblem(pb; c, h = hsat, N = n, ε, tspan = (0.0, 730.0)))
alive(r) = count(r.alive) / length(r.alive)

@printf("frogs needed for loads to run away: %.0f\n", host_density_threshold(pb))
r0 = tipping(0.0)
step!("Bd frog", "host", "Briggs 2010 load model", alive(r0), NaN, "all die: 80 frogs is above the threshold of 23")
```

#### Step 1. Frogs clear some of their load

Frogs have defences. Here each frog removes sporangia at a rate that saturates as load rises:
defences cope with a light infection and are overwhelmed by a heavy one (this package's load
tipping model; the clearance values are illustrative).

```{julia}
c = 100.0
@printf("frogs needed for loads to run away: %d\n", critical_host_number(pb; c, h = hsat, ε))
r1 = tipping(c)
r1small = tipping(c; n = 50)
@printf("alive after two years: %.2f of 80 frogs, %.2f of 50 frogs\n", alive(r1), alive(r1small))
step!("Bd frog", "host", "+ saturating clearance by the frog", alive(r1), NaN,
    "threshold rises from 23 to 68 frogs; 80 still all die")
```

#### Step 2. Frogs differ

Frogs now differ in how strong their defences are (lognormal, same median). Treatment starts
at step 3, on these frogs: each frog, with probability 0.4, carries bacteria that triple its
clearance, for life.

```{julia}
# in random order, so that a group made of the first frogs is a random sample
cs = shuffle(Xoshiro(2), quantile.(LogNormal(log(c), 0.5), ((1:N) .- 0.5) ./ N))
r2 = tipping(cs)
frogs(tr; kw...) = solve(ProbioticLoadProblem(pb, tr; c = cs, c_treated = 3 .* cs, h = hsat, N, ε,
    days = 730, kw...); rng = Xoshiro(1))
ref_c = frogs(T(); coverage = 0.4)
step!("Bd frog", "host", "+ frogs differ in their defences", alive(r2), NaN,
    "a few of the best-defended survive")
```

With identical frogs a die-off is all or nothing; with differences it is partial, and it
stops when too few frogs are left to sustain the pool. The treatment steps keep these
differences: a treated frog clears sporangia three times as fast as it would untreated.

### Treatment

#### Step 3. A treated class

Treated frogs clear sporangia faster. In the load equations above, frog $i$ (with its own
clearance $c_i$ from step 2) clears at

$$
\tilde c_i = \begin{cases} 3 c_i, & \text{frog } i \text{ treated}, \\ c_i, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}
$$

On day 0 each frog is treated with probability equal to the coverage, so the treated frogs
differ from run to run. Loads follow the equations through each day. At the end of each day
a treated frog stops being treated with probability $1 - e^{-\omega}$, where
$\omega = \ln 2 / t_{1/2}$. In step 3, $t_{1/2}$ is infinite (treated for life); step 4 sets
$t_{1/2} = 30$ days. The package can also let untreated frogs pick up the bacteria from
treated ones; that is switched off here.

| Symbol | Meaning | Value or source |
|---|---|---|
| $\tilde c_i$ | clearance of frog $i$, treated or not | $3 c_i$ when treated (median 300 sporangia per day); illustrative |
| coverage | probability that a frog is treated on day 0 | 0.4; illustrative |
| $t_{1/2}$ | half-life of the treated state | infinite (step 3), 30 days (step 4); illustrative |

```{julia}
step!("Bd frog", "treatment", "treated class: 40% of frogs, lasts for life", alive(r2),
    ref_c.alive[end] / N, "all survive, including the untreated: protection is shared")
```

Because disease depends on the shared pool, treating 40% protects everyone.

#### Step 4. Protection is lost

```{julia}
a = frogs(T(half_life = 30.0); coverage = 0.4)
@printf("first death: day %d (untreated: day %d)\n", minimum(filter(>(0), a.death_day)),
    ceil(Int, minimum(filter(!isnan, r2.death_time))))
step!("Bd frog", "treatment", "+ protection lost, half-life 30 days", alive(r2), a.alive[end] / N,
    "die-off delayed by about two months, not prevented")
```

#### Step 5. Bacteria as a state of each frog

Until now every treated animal has been simply "treated", and lost protection all at once.
Each frog now carries its own abundance of the applied bacteria, which declines with the
half-life fitted to field data (5 days; this project's own fit), and its protection wanes with
it. This replaces the treated class and its 30-day loss with a more realistic version of the
same thing; the coverage (40% of frogs) and the size of the effect stay.

In equations, each frog $i$ now carries an abundance $B_i$ of the applied bacteria, in dose
units. A bath sets $B_i = 1$ on every live frog in the bathed group (the first 40% of frogs,
32 of 80; the frogs are in random order). Between baths

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dB_i}{dt} &= -\delta B_i + x\,(\bar{B} - B_i),
  \qquad \delta = \frac{\ln 2}{t_B},
  \qquad \bar{B} = \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{alive}}}\sum_{j\ \mathrm{alive}} B_j, \\
\tilde c_i &= c_i + (3c_i - c_i)\,\frac{B_i}{B_i + 1/F},
\end{aligned}
$$

and $S_i$ and $Z$ follow the equations of step 0 with clearance $\tilde c_i$. The exchange
rate $x$ is 0 in this step and is added in step 6. With $F = 100$ a freshly bathed frog has 99%
of the extra clearance, and keeps at least half of it until $B_i$ falls to $1/F$: about
$\log_2 F \approx 6.6$ half-lives (33 days) without exchange. Step 7 repeats the bath on days
0, 90, 180, and so on.

| Symbol | Meaning | Value or source |
|---|---|---|
| $B_i$ | abundance of applied bacteria on frog $i$ | state (dose units; 1 just after a bath) |
| $t_B$ | half-life of the abundance | 5 days; this package's fit to field data, not a published estimate |
| $x$ | rate at which frogs exchange bacteria | 0 in step 5; 0.1 per day from step 6, chosen to match the field ratio |
| $F$ | protective fold: abundance after a bath divided by the abundance giving half the effect | 100; illustrative |
| $3c_i$ | clearance of frog $i$ at full effect | as in step 3; illustrative |
| coverage | share of frogs bathed | 0.4, as in step 3; illustrative |

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Bacteria on frog $i$: set to 1 by a bath, lost at rate δ, exchanged with other frogs (from step 6), and raising the clearance of sporangia (dashed)."
diagram("""
digraph {
  bath [label = "bath\\n(days 0, 90, …)", shape = plaintext, style = ""];
  Bi [label = <bacteria B<SUB>i</SUB><BR/>on frog i>, fillcolor = "#cfe2f3"];
  Bj [label = <other frogs B<SUB>j</SUB>>, fillcolor = "#cfe2f3"];
  lostB [label = "lost", shape = plaintext, style = ""];
  Si [label = <sporangia S<SUB>i</SUB><BR/>on frog i>];
  Z [label = "zoospores Z", shape = ellipse, fillcolor = "#e2efda"];
  lostS [label = "lost", shape = plaintext, style = ""];
  bath -> Bi [label = <sets B<SUB>i</SUB> = 1>];
  Bi -> lostB [label = <δB<SUB>i</SUB>>];
  Bi -> Bj [dir = both, label = <exchange<BR/>x(B̄ − B<SUB>i</SUB>)>];
  Bi -> Si [style = dashed, color = "#888888", fontcolor = "#666666",
            label = <raises clearance<BR/>from c<SUB>i</SUB> toward 3c<SUB>i</SUB>>];
  Z -> Si [label = "(νγ/V) Z"];
  Si -> Z [label = <η(1−f) S<SUB>i</SUB>>];
  Si -> lostS [label = <σS<SUB>i</SUB> + c<SUB>i</SUB>S<SUB>i</SUB>/(h + S<SUB>i</SUB>)>];
}
""")
```

```{julia}
baths(; x = 0.1, F = 100.0, coverage = 0.4, dose_days = [0], days = 730) =
    solve(ProbioticAbundanceProblem(pb, T(abundance_half_life = 5.0, protective_fold = F, direct = x);
        c = cs, c_treated = 3 .* cs, h = hsat, N, ε, coverage, dose_days, days))
first_death(r) = any(>(0), r.death_day) ? minimum(filter(>(0), r.death_day)) : 0
alone = baths(x = 0.0)
@printf("first death: day %d\n", first_death(alone))
step!("Bd frog", "treatment", "bacteria on each frog, fitted decay; one bath", alive(r2),
    alone.alive[end] / N, "die-off delayed by about four weeks")
```

#### Step 6. The bacteria spread between frogs

Frogs exchange bacteria through the pond. Exchange moves bacteria between frogs without
creating any, so they spread but do not sustain themselves: summed over live frogs the
exchange terms cancel, and the mean abundance falls at rate $\delta$ whatever $x$ is. That is
what the field trial showed: eleven days after most frogs in a pond were bathed, frogs that
were never bathed carried about 0.63 times as much of the bacterium as bathed ones, and it
then declined in both. To compare like with like, the exchange rate is chosen by bathing 75% of
frogs, as in the trial:

```{julia}
for x in (0.0, 0.1, 1.0)
    r = baths(; x, coverage = 0.75, days = 30)
    @printf("exchange %.1f per day: unbathed/bathed abundance on day 11 = %.2f\n", x,
        r.abundance_unbathed[12] / r.abundance_bathed[12])
end
```

An exchange rate of about 0.1 per day comes close to the field ratio and is used from here on.

```{julia}
one = baths()
@printf("first death: day %d\n", first_death(one))
step!("Bd frog", "treatment", "+ bacteria spread between frogs", alive(r2),
    one.alive[end] / N, "little change: spread shares the bacteria but makes no more")
```

#### Step 7. Repeated baths

```{julia}
untreated, every90 = baths(coverage = 0.0), baths(dose_days = 0:90:729)
plot(untreated.t, max.(untreated.mean_load, 1.0); yscale = :log10, label = "no treatment",
    xlabel = "days", ylabel = "mean Bd load per live frog", legend = :bottomright, xlims = (0, 730))
plot!(one.t, max.(one.mean_load, 1.0); label = "one bath on day 0")
plot!(every90.t, max.(every90.mean_load, 1.0); label = "a bath every 90 days")
hline!([pb.Smax]; color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "lethal load")
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("| Baths | Alive after 2 years (of 80) | First death (day) |")
println("|---|---|---|")
for (label, r) in (("none", untreated), ("one, day 0", one), ("every 240 days", baths(dose_days = 0:240:729)),
        ("every 150 days", baths(dose_days = 0:150:729)), ("every 90 days", every90),
        ("every 90 days, 10% of frogs", baths(coverage = 0.1, dose_days = 0:90:729)),
        ("every 90 days, 10% of frogs, no exchange", baths(coverage = 0.1, x = 0.0, dose_days = 0:90:729)),
        ("one, day 150 (loads already high)", baths(dose_days = [150])))
    @printf("| %s | %d | %s |\n", label, r.alive[end], first_death(r) == 0 ? "none" : string(first_death(r)))
end
```

```{julia}
step!("Bd frog", "treatment", "+ a bath every 90 days", alive(r2), every90.alive[end] / N,
    "all survive: each bath resets the slow build-up of load")
```

This is the one system where bacteria that last only weeks could still work. Load takes
months to build; a short burst of extra clearance knocks it back, and the build-up starts
again. Because frogs exchange bacteria, bathing a small part of the population protects the
rest.

#### Step 8. Chance

The same model with every sporangium on every frog, and every zoospore in the pool, a whole
number, and every event random (`StochasticFrogProblem`); 20 runs of each case. The frogs keep
their own clearances, and 40% of them are bathed.

Time moves in steps of $dt = 0.05$ days. In each step the random events have the rates of
the equations, so on average they follow them:

| Event in a step | Number drawn | Term in the equations |
|---|---|---|
| new sporangia on frog $i$ | Poisson with mean $\left(\frac{\nu\gamma}{V} Z + \eta\nu f S_i\right) dt$ | first two terms of $dS_i/dt$ |
| sporangia lost from frog $i$ | Binomial($S_i$, $1 - e^{-(\sigma + c_i/(h + S_i))\,dt}$) | $\sigma S_i + c_i S_i/(h + S_i)$ |
| zoospores released by frog $i$ | Poisson with mean $\eta(1 - f) S_i\,dt$ | $\eta(1 - f)\sum_j S_j$ |
| zoospores lost from the pool | Binomial($Z$, $1 - e^{-(\mu + \gamma N_{\mathrm{alive}}/V)\,dt}$) | $\mu Z + (\gamma/V) N_{\mathrm{alive}} Z$ |
| zoospores from outside | Poisson with mean $\varepsilon\,dt$ | $\varepsilon$ |

A frog dies as soon as $S_i$ reaches $S_{\max}$. The bacteria $B_i$ stay continuous and follow
the equation of steps 5 and 6, solved exactly over each step.

```{julia}
bath_tr = T(abundance_half_life = 5.0, protective_fold = 100.0, direct = 0.1)
chanceC(; tr = bath_tr, kw...) = [solve(StochasticFrogProblem(pb, tr; c = cs, c_treated = 3 .* cs, h = hsat,
    N, ε, days = 730, coverage = 0.4, kw...); rng = Xoshiro(s)) for s in 1:20]
aliveC(rs) = sum(r.alive[end] for r in rs) / (N * length(rs))
firstC(rs) = (v = sort([first_death(r) for r in rs if first_death(r) > 0]); isempty(v) ? "none" : string(v[cld(length(v), 2)]))
cases = [("no treatment", chanceC(coverage = 0.0), untreated),
    ("bath every 90 days", chanceC(dose_days = 0:90:729), every90),
    ("bath every 150 days", chanceC(dose_days = 0:150:729), baths(dose_days = 0:150:729)),
    ("bath every 90 days, 10% of frogs", chanceC(coverage = 0.1, dose_days = 0:90:729),
        baths(coverage = 0.1, dose_days = 0:90:729))]
nothing
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("| Baths | Equations: alive after 2 years | Chance: alive (mean of 20 runs) | Chance: runs with no deaths | Chance: median first death |")
println("|---|---|---|---|---|")
for (label, rs, det) in cases
    @printf("| %s | %d | %.0f | %d of 20 | %s |\n", label, det.alive[end], aliveC(rs) * N,
        count(r -> r.alive[end] == N, rs), firstC(rs))
end
```

```{julia}
step!("Bd frog", "chance", "+ chance: whole sporangia and zoospores", aliveC(cases[1][2]), aliveC(cases[2][2]),
    "baths every 90 days still protect; less frequent or narrower bathing now fails")
```

Chance makes the frog system harder to protect: a few frogs whose loads happen to run high
feed the shared pool and tip the rest. Baths every 90 days still protect every frog in every
run, but baths every 150 days, which were enough in the equations, now fail, and so does
bathing 10% of frogs, in every run.

Two cautions. The slow build-up is for a population that starts clean. In the field trial the
pond was in the middle of an outbreak, treated frogs were surrounded by heavily infected ones,
and their loads were back within two months; the last row of the table is the model's version
of treating too late. And the size of the clearance effect of the bacteria is assumed, not
measured.

## How much did each step move the answer?

The change in the treated outcome at each step, for each system. Bars to the right are steps
that made treatment look better; bars to the left, worse.

```{julia}
function change_plot(system)
    rows = filter(r -> r.system == system && !isnan(r.treated), ladder)
    d = [rows[i].treated - rows[i - 1].treated for i in 2:length(rows)]
    labels = ["$(rows[i].n). $(rows[i].added)" for i in 2:length(rows)]
    bar(d; orientation = :h, yticks = (1:length(d), labels), yflip = true, legend = false,
        xlims = (-1.05, 1.05), xlabel = "change in treated outcome", title = system,
        color = [x >= 0 ? :seagreen : :indianred for x in d], left_margin = 6Plots.mm,
        size = (840, 70 + 34 * length(d)))
    vline!([0.0]; color = :black)
end
change_plot("Bsal")
```

```{julia}
change_plot("Bd toad")
```

```{julia}
change_plot("Bd frog")
```

Large bars point both ways in every system. No single addition dominates, and the sign of a
step depends on the system: the observed mechanism (survive, still infected) is the largest
negative step for Bsal and a positive step for toads.

## Does the effect of one piece of realism depend on the others?

A ladder adds things in one order. To check that the order is not driving the conclusions,
four pieces of treatment realism are switched on and off in every combination for Bsal, on
the full host model of step 3:

- **mechanism**: blocks infection (0.99), or survive but stay infected (0.99);
- **duration**: lasts for life, or fitted decay (half-life 5 days);
- **spread**: none, or between animals at 50 per year;
- **stages**: adults once, or both stages every quarter with the bacteria kept through
  metamorphosis.

```{julia}
levels = (
    mechanism = ["blocks", "survive"],
    duration = ["lasting", "decays"],
    spread = ["none", "spreads"],
    stages = ["adults", "both"],
)
function factorial_run(mech, dur, spr, stg)
    tr = T(; (mech == "blocks" ? (efficacy = 0.99,) : (tolerance = 0.99,))...,
        (dur == "decays" ? (abundance_half_life = 5 / 365, protective_fold = 100.0) : (;))...,
        direct = spr == "spreads" ? 50.0 : 0.0)
    kw = stg == "both" ? (treat = :both, treat_times = quarterly, retention = 1.0) : (;)
    return lar(stage, tr; coverage = 1.0, kw...).mean_adults
end
design = [(; mech, dur, spr, stg, outcome = factorial_run(mech, dur, spr, stg))
          for mech in levels.mechanism, dur in levels.duration, spr in levels.spread, stg in levels.stages]
design = sort(vec(design); by = r -> -r.outcome)
nothing
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
println("| Mechanism | Duration | Spread | Stages treated | Mean adults |")
println("|---|---|---|---|---|")
for r in design
    @printf("| %s | %s | %s | %s | %.2f |\n", r.mech, r.dur, r.spr, r.stg, r.outcome)
end
```

The average effect of switching each piece on, and how much that effect varies with the
other three:

```{julia}
#| output: asis
function effect(field, on)
    diffs = Float64[]
    for r in design
        getfield(r, field) == on || continue
        partner = only(filter(q -> all(getfield(q, f) == getfield(r, f) for f in (:mech, :dur, :spr, :stg) if f != field) &&
            getfield(q, field) != on, design))
        push!(diffs, r.outcome - partner.outcome)
    end
    return diffs
end
println("| Switched on | Mean change | Smallest | Largest |")
println("|---|---|---|---|")
for (field, on, label) in ((:mech, "survive", "survive instead of block"), (:dur, "decays", "fitted decay"),
        (:spr, "spreads", "spread between animals"), (:stg, "both", "treat both stages"))
    d = effect(field, on)
    @printf("| %s | %+.2f | %+.2f | %+.2f |\n", label, sum(d) / length(d), minimum(d), maximum(d))
end
```

The ranges are wide: the effect of each piece depends strongly on the others. Spread, for
example, matters a great deal for a lasting, infection-blocking treatment given to adults,
and hardly at all once the bacteria decay in days. (In the model, animals that acquire
bacteria from others share the dosing clock of the treated ones, so spread cannot outlast the
decay.) A piece of realism therefore cannot be judged by adding it to a simple model alone.

## All steps

```{julia}
#| output: asis
fmt(x) = isnan(x) ? "" : @sprintf("%.2f", x)
println("| System | Step | Phase | Added | No treatment | With treatment | What changed |")
println("|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|")
for r in ladder
    println("| ", join((r.system, r.n, r.phase, r.added, fmt(r.untreated), fmt(r.treated), r.note), " | "), " |")
end
```

## What the exercise shows

1. **The answer changed at almost every step, and reversed more than once.** For Bsal, a
   model stopped at step 5 says a self-spreading microbiome protects fully; at step 6, the
   effect seen in trials makes the same treatment fail; treating larvae as well (step 8) does
   not rescue it, although it would protect fully with bacteria that blocked infection; and at
   step 9 bacteria that last a few weeks fail whatever else is done.
2. **Host biology can move the answer as much as treatment biology, but not everywhere.** A
   larval stage changed the untreated fate of the salamanders. One survival probability for
   infected toad metamorphs reversed both the untreated outcome and the value of the
   reference treatment. The [second vignette](../02_nested_model/02_nested_model.md) tests
   this like for like in a single model and finds that it depends on the regime: for Bsal at
   the published host density, six pieces of host biology barely change the outcome, and
   near the invasion threshold they change it a great deal. Its stochastic version also
   shows that chance can matter more than any of them: with whole animals, blocking
   infection in every adult on arrival nearly always eliminates Bsal, where the equations
   of step 1 here leave about a third of the population.
3. **How protection works matters more than how strong it is, and its effect has no fixed
   sign.** Letting animals survive infection is the worst change for Bsal and an improvement
   for toads.
4. **Effects interact.** The factorial shows that the value of spread, of treating larvae or
   of a lasting treatment each depends on the other pieces.
5. **The systems differ for structural reasons.** A toad cohort passes through a short
   infected stage once a year and can be re-treated. A salamander must be protected for life
   against a pathogen that kills in a week. In frogs, where disease follows a load that
   builds slowly, short-lived bacteria can still work if they are re-applied.
6. **Chance is a piece of realism, and it changed the answer in every system, in different
   directions.** For Bsal it made the reference treatment, which blocks infection, protect
   nearly the whole population, because Bsal arriving among treated animals is lost before it
   can establish; it did not rescue the final treatment, which does not block infection. For
   toads it overturned
   the published extinction of both host and pathogen. For frogs it made treatment harder,
   because random high loads tip the population sooner.

## What is not in the models

- In Parts A and B bacterial abundance is a clock since the last dose, not a state of each
  animal. Only the frog model of Part C tracks it per animal.
- The fold-drop in abundance at which protection is lost has not been measured, nor has the
  effect of the bacteria on clearance, nor whether applied bacteria survive metamorphosis.
- The Bsal model has no recovery from infection and no years between metamorphosis and
  maturity. The toad model has thresholds standing in for extinction, and adult toads are
  never treated.
- The three systems do not share one model structure, so Part B starts from a more complex
  model than Part A. The [second vignette](../02_nested_model/02_nested_model.md) uses one
  nested model, for the salamander system, in which every piece of biology is a switch.
- No fade-out rule is applied in Part A, so densities can fall to meaningless values and
  recover. The second vignette shows what such a rule changes.
- The stochastic steps use one introduced infected animal (Part A) or the published
  introduction (Parts B and C), one population size, and time steps of hours to a day. In
  Part A the area is 20 hectares; whether the host is lost depends on it (see the second
  vignette).
